opus-5.5.text:
I think it really depends on the stage of the project and what kind of problem you're trying to solve.

In research, especially in the early, exploratory phase, I lean quite heavily toward bottom-up. The people closest to the problem, the researchers actually running experiments and reading papers every day, often have the best intuition about what's promising. If I dictate everything from the top, I'm basically capping the team's ideas at my own imagination, and that's a very low ceiling. Many of the most interesting things we've done started because someone on the team was curious about something and we gave them room to try it.

But bottom-up has a limitation. When everyone follows their own curiosity, you get a lot of small, scattered efforts. Each might produce a nice paper, but none of them gets big enough to really matter. The field has changed a lot in the last few years. Building something like a world foundation model is not a one- or two-person project. You need data pipelines, large-scale training infrastructure, evaluation, tokenizers, post-training, all moving together. At that point you need a clear top-down direction: this is the goal, this is the timeline, and these are the pieces that have to fit together.

So the way I think about it is roughly this. Top-down for the "what" and the "why": setting the big mission and making sure we concentrate our resources instead of spreading them thin. Bottom-up for the "how": within that mission, people have a lot of freedom to propose approaches, challenge assumptions, and own their piece.

The hard part as a manager is knowing when to switch. If you go top-down too early, you lock into a direction before you understand the problem, and you can miss a better path. If you stay bottom-up too long, you miss the window, because in this field things move very fast and someone else will scale up the idea first. A lot of my job is sensing that moment: we've explored enough, the signal is clear, now let's commit and push together.

I'd also say trust matters a lot. Top-down only works if people believe the direction is right and understand the reasoning. So even when I'm making a top-down call, I try to explain why, and listen when people push back. Often the best pushback comes from the most junior people, because they're closest to the details.

r001.rationale: The response says the choice depends on the project’s stage and the problem to solve, and describes switching approaches as the team’s needs change.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I actually think the dichotomy is a bit of a false one. In practice I don't really choose between them; I use both, and the real question is what gets decided from the top and what gets decided from the bottom.

What I try to set from the top is the direction and the standard. For a research team, that means being very clear about what problem we are trying to solve, why it matters, and what "good" looks like. If I'm vague about that, people drift, and you end up with ten interesting projects that don't add up to anything. So on the question of "where are we going," I'm fairly top-down, and I'm honest about it. I'll say, this is the bet we're making, and here is my reasoning.

But how we get there, that's where I want things to come from the bottom. The people doing the work are much closer to the details than I am. They know which idea is actually working, which experiment is failing, which assumption I made from a distance is wrong. If I try to micromanage the how, I'm essentially throwing away the information advantage of having smart people on the team. So I try to give a lot of freedom there, and I try to make it easy for someone to come back and tell me, "the direction you set doesn't make sense, and here is the evidence."

The thing that makes this work is that the top-down part has to be open to being overturned by the bottom-up part. If I set a direction and then refuse to update when the people doing the work bring back evidence, then I'm not really doing both; I'm just doing top-down with extra steps. So I think of it as: I set the hypothesis, the team runs the experiment, and the experiment is allowed to prove me wrong.

It also depends on the stage. When a team is new, or when a project is very early and nobody knows what the right question is yet, I lean more top-down, because somebody has to put a stake in the ground. Once the team has momentum and people have built their own intuition about the problem, I pull back and let more of it come from them. If you never make that transition, you end up with a team that waits for you on everything, and that doesn't scale. And if you make it too early, you get chaos. So a lot of the judgment is really about reading where the team is.

r001.rationale: The response says the balance depends on the team’s stage, leaning more top-down when the team or project is new and pulling back as the team gains momentum.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on the team and the problem you’re trying to solve. In research, you need room for bottom-up ideas because the people doing the work often see opportunities that a manager won’t see. If you prescribe every step, you lose a lot of that creativity.

But you also need a clear direction. People should understand what we’re trying to achieve, why it matters, and what constraints we have. That’s where I think top-down management is useful: setting priorities and making decisions when there are competing goals.

So I would combine the two. Align on the goal, give people ownership of how to get there, and check in often enough to learn and adjust. If the problem is very uncertain, give exploration more space. If there’s a clear deliverable and a tight deadline, be more explicit about coordination. The balance should change with the situation.

r001.rationale: The response says the choice depends on the team and problem, and that the balance should change with the situation, conveying that it should be tailored to what the team needs at that time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on the decision and where the information is. If the people doing the work understand the problem best, you want ideas and decisions to come from them. If you make every decision from the top, you lose that knowledge, and people stop taking ownership.

But leadership still has to provide direction: What are we trying to achieve? What matters most? What constraints do we have? Without that clarity, bottom-up work can become a collection of interesting projects that don’t add up.

So I would combine the two: set a clear direction, give people room to figure out how to get there, and keep talking as you learn. The balance can change. When there’s a lot of uncertainty, you need room for exploration. When the team needs to commit and execute together, you need more alignment.

r001.rationale: The response says the balance depends on the decision and the team's circumstances, and can change between exploration and execution, conveying that the choice should fit what the team needs at the time.
